overview.title: Training the embedding LSTM: smaller and faster, but still 84%
overview.main_topic: The embedding LSTM's totals (1,986,177 parameters), Listing 14.25 (training and evaluation, test accuracy 0.84436), why accuracy did not improve (not enough data to learn a good embedding; overfitting, with train accuracy above 99%), the motivation for pretraining, and the start of the sidebar on text augmentation
overview.central_idea: Replacing one-hot inputs with a learned Embedding layer makes the model roughly 10× smaller and faster, but accuracy stays at about 84%, because 20,000 reviews are too few to learn good embeddings before the model overfits. The fix is to pretrain the embedding separately on more, unlabeled data.
overview.importance: It separates efficiency from accuracy: embeddings solve the efficiency problem, but quality is limited by data. That motivates pretraining (14.5.4), the idea behind modern NLP.
learning_objectives: Compare the size and accuracy of the one-hot and embedding LSTMs
Read Listing 14.25 and interpret its result
Explain why a learned embedding did not raise accuracy here
Explain the idea of pretraining an embedding without labels
Know why text augmentation is less used than image augmentation (sidebar, begun)

summary:
The top of the page finishes the model summary from p.436: **Total params 1,986,177 (7.58 MB)**, all trainable. The authors note that the parameter count fell from **15 million to 2 million** compared with the one-hot LSTM.

**Listing 14.25** trains the model exactly as before (`sequence_train_ds`, validation on `sequence_val_ds`, `epochs=10`, `callbacks=[early_stopping]`) and evaluates it on `sequence_test_ds`. Test accuracy: **0.8443599939346313**.

The embedding cut both **training time and model size by an order of magnitude**, so a learned embedding is clearly far more efficient than one-hot encoding. **However, accuracy did not change.** It stayed stubbornly around **84%**, far from the bag-of-words (88%) and bigram (90%) models.

Does that mean structured embeddings aren't useful, or aren't useful for classification? **Quite the contrary**: a well-trained embedding can dramatically raise a model's performance ceiling. The problem here is the **training setup**. The **20,000 training reviews** are not enough to learn a good word embedding. By the end of training, **train accuracy exceeds 99%**: the model has started to **overfit and memorize** before it has learned an optimal set of embeddings.

The remedy is **pretraining**: train the embedding **separately, on more data**, without needing positive/negative labels, instead of jointly with the classifier.

A sidebar, **"Augmenting text data"**, begins. Since augmentation was so important for vision, can it be done for text? Yes, but it is **not nearly as effective**. Basic techniques make small edits to the input text to improve robustness, for example random deletion of words (continued on p.438, which also covers swapping words, the risk of changing meaning, synonym replacement and generative augmentation).

paragraphs.what_it_says: A well-trained embedding can dramatically improve the performance ceiling. The issue is the training setup: 20,000 reviews are not enough to learn a good embedding. By the end of training, train accuracy is above 99%. The model overfits and memorizes before it learns optimal embeddings.

concepts.name: Overfitting
concepts.definition: Fitting the training data (here >99% accuracy) far better than unseen data (about 84%).
concepts.intuition: Memorizing the answers to the practice questions instead of learning the subject.
concepts.technical: A large model (2M parameters) trained on few examples (20,000) learns its classifier quickly and stops improving its embeddings.
concepts.significance: It is the authors' diagnosis of why embeddings did not help.
concepts.example: Train accuracy above 99% after 10 epochs vs. 0.844 test accuracy.
concepts.misconception: Overfitting does not mean the architecture is bad; it can mean the data is insufficient.

concepts.name: Pretraining
concepts.definition: Training a component, here the word embedding, separately on more data and without task labels, then reusing it.
concepts.intuition: Learning vocabulary by reading many books before taking a reading-comprehension test.
concepts.technical: Unsupervised or self-supervised objectives on large unlabeled corpora produce embeddings that initialize the classifier.
concepts.significance: It is the remedy for the data-constrained embedding; chapter 15 extends it to whole Transformers.
concepts.example: Training word vectors on large amounts of text, then using them for IMDb (p.438 onward).
concepts.misconception: Pretraining does not need labeled sentiment data.

concepts.name: Word embedding
concepts.technical: Here it is learned jointly with the classifier from 20,000 reviews, which is too little data.
concepts.significance: Efficient, but its quality depends on the amount of data.
concepts.misconception: Switching to embeddings automatically improves accuracy. Here it only improved efficiency.

concepts.name: Text data augmentation
concepts.definition: Generating modified versions of input text (deletions, swaps, synonyms) to make a model more robust.
concepts.intuition: Practicing on slightly garbled versions of the same sentence.
concepts.technical: Unlike image transforms, text edits often change the label-relevant meaning.
concepts.significance: The authors say it works, but much less well than in vision.
concepts.misconception: Augmentation is not as safe or as effective for text as for images.

deeper.title: Efficiency vs. accuracy: why both models land at 84%
deeper.body: The one-hot LSTM multiplied one-hot vectors by its input kernels, which is mathematically a per-word lookup of a 256-dimensional projection, per direction. So it too learned something like an embedding, just stored wastefully inside each gate. The Embedding model factorizes this into one shared 64-dimensional vector per word followed by a small LSTM. Both have to learn the word representations from the same 20,000 labeled reviews, so it is unsurprising that they hit the same ceiling. The bottleneck is information (data), not computation. (This analysis is ours; the book's diagnosis is the data limitation.)

deeper.title: How pretraining helps
deeper.body:
1. Collect a large unlabeled corpus (many more words than IMDb's 20,000 training reviews).
2. Train embeddings on a self-supervised objective, such as predicting a word from its context, so that the vectors encode general word similarity.
3. Load these vectors into the classifier's Embedding layer.
4. Train the classifier on the labeled reviews. It no longer has to discover word meanings from scratch, so it overfits less.
The book implements this in 14.5.4-14.5.5 (pp.438-443) and reports that it brings the LSTM roughly level with the set models.

deeper.title: Learning a language from 20,000 movie reviews
deeper.body: Asking the model to learn word meanings from 20,000 labeled reviews is like learning a foreign language only from the grade stamps on 20,000 essays. You will memorize which essays got good grades long before you understand the words. Reading lots of unlabeled text first (pretraining) gives you the vocabulary.

misconceptions.claim: Since accuracy did not improve, word embeddings are not useful for text classification.
misconceptions.correction: The authors say the opposite: a well-trained embedding can dramatically raise the ceiling. Here it was undertrained because of limited data.

misconceptions.claim: The embedding model is slightly worse (84.4% vs 84.8%), so one-hot is better.
misconceptions.correction: The difference is within run-to-run noise; the book says performance "did not change". The embedding model is far more efficient.

misconceptions.claim: Text augmentation is as effective as image augmentation.
misconceptions.correction: The sidebar says it is not nearly as effective, because small edits can change the meaning of text (more on p.438).

takeaways: The embedding LSTM has 1,986,177 parameters versus about 15.4M for the one-hot version.
Listing 14.25 gives 0.84436 test accuracy, the same as before (about 84%).
Embeddings fixed efficiency (size and training time), not accuracy.
Diagnosis: 20,000 reviews are too few to learn good embeddings; train accuracy exceeds 99%, so the model overfits first.
Remedy: pretrain embeddings separately on more, unlabeled data.
Text augmentation exists but is much less effective than image augmentation.

questions.question: What test accuracy does Listing 14.25 report?
questions.explanation: That is the printed output. 0.84811 is the one-hot LSTM (p.432), 0.90116 the bigram model (p.428), and 99% is the training accuracy, not test accuracy.

questions.question: Why, according to the authors, did the embedding not improve accuracy?
questions.answer: The 20,000 training reviews are too few to learn a good word embedding. The model overfits (train accuracy above 99%) before it learns optimal embeddings.
questions.explanation: The authors blame the training setup (data), not the concept of embeddings.

questions.question: What does pretraining mean here, and what does it not require?
questions.answer: Training the word embedding separately, on more data, instead of jointly with the classifier. It does not require positive/negative review labels.
questions.explanation: This is stated in the last paragraph before the sidebar.

questions.question: By what factor did the parameter count shrink (15,393,409 → 1,986,177)? Is "an order of magnitude" accurate?
questions.answer: About 7.75×. That is roughly, but not quite, an order of magnitude (10×).

questions.question: Which improvement did the Embedding layer clearly bring?
options: Much smaller model and faster training
Higher test accuracy than the bigram model
questions.answer: Much smaller model and faster training
questions.explanation: The page says size and training time fell by an order of magnitude. Accuracy stayed at about 84% (below bigrams at 90%), the model still overfits, and padding is still used, now masked.

questions.question: According to the sidebar, how effective is text augmentation compared with image augmentation, and what is one basic technique?
questions.answer: It works but is not nearly as effective. Example: randomly deleting words (or swapping them, p.438).
questions.explanation: The sidebar begins on this page and continues on p.438.

questions.question: Could you explain to someone why a more efficient model is not automatically a more accurate one, using this page's experiment?
questions.answer: Efficiency comes from a better representation of the input; accuracy is limited by how much information the training data provides. Both LSTMs had to learn word representations from the same 20,000 reviews.
questions.explanation: Revisit the paragraphs "However..." and "Quite the contrary...".
